speaker: April Dunford
title: How to nail your product positioning | April Dunford (Obviously Awesome)
question: In B2B software, is clear product differentiation always necessary to win deals, or can you win without it?
guest: You want to take a customer's viewpoint and look at how B2B buying actually works. A VP of sales wakes up and says, "The way we track our pipeline sucks, we need a CRM." They don't go look for it themselves—they tap a sales ops manager to find one. That person isn't an expert on the CRM market, so they search online, hit review sites with thousands of tools all claiming to be in the top-right quadrant, and have no idea how to build a shortlist. More importantly, they have to go back and justify their choice to their boss. You can't tell your VP, "They were all the same, I just liked the rep." You need to explain why you made a smart choice. The best thing a vendor can do on a sales call is lay out how the market shakes out—which tools fit big enterprises, which fit other use cases, and why a buyer with their exact needs requires your specific capabilities. If you can't help them feel confident justifying that decision, they go back to their boss and say, "Let's just keep using the spreadsheet." Around forty percent of the time, deals end in no decision—nobody gets the deal.

points.core: Mid-level buyers tasked with vendor research rarely possess deep category expertise.
points.note: Accept: an executive delegates software evaluation to a non-expert manager who gets overwhelmed by crowded review sites and indistinguishable vendors. Do not credit: generic claims that software markets are competitive.

points.core: Internal buyers must justify a defensible vendor choice to their leadership.
points.note: Accept: the buyer cannot tell their boss they picked randomly or just liked the rep; they need a concrete rationale showing they made a smart choice. Do not credit: generic mentions of ROI or budget approval.

points.core: Undifferentiated vendors push uncertain buyers toward making no purchase decision.
points.note: Accept: when options look identical, buyers stall, stick with spreadsheets or the status quo, and nobody wins the deal (around 40% of B2B deals). Do not credit: claiming undifferentiated products simply lose on price.

points.core: Effective vendors map market tradeoffs to show fit for specific buyer needs.
points.note: Accept: explaining which competitors fit other segments versus which specific capabilities make your product the right choice for this buyer's profile. Do not credit: vague advice to highlight unique features or brand storytelling.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
No, clear product differentiation is not always necessary; plenty of B2B deals are won without it, though you still need some reason for the buyer to choose you.

In mature categories (CRM, HR software, security tools), buyers often see the shortlisted products as roughly equivalent. What decides the deal then is usually something other than features: a better sales experience, stronger relationships and trust, perceived lower risk, brand reputation, pricing and commercial terms, implementation and support quality, existing integrations, or simply being present earlier and shaping the buying criteria. Research on B2B buying has repeatedly found that the sales experience itself and risk reduction weigh heavily, since buyers fear making a bad decision more than they value a marginal feature advantage.

That said, winning without product differentiation has costs. You face more price pressure, depend more on sales execution and distribution, and are vulnerable to a competitor who does differentiate or who undercuts you.

So differentiation of some kind is necessary, but it need not live in the product. It can come from who you serve, how you sell, how you deliver, or how safe you are to choose.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Clear product differentiation is not always necessary to win B2B software deals. Companies routinely win with functionally similar products by outperforming competitors on distribution, commercial terms, and risk reduction. In mature categories like payroll, ticketing, or standard CRM, core features quickly converge, and buyers rarely need unique capabilities to solve everyday operational problems.

Without a distinct product edge, vendors win through superior sales execution, faster responsiveness, flexible pricing, and frictionless procurement. Incumbents frequently beat best-of-breed rivals by bundling a "good enough" tool into an existing contract, sparing the buyer another security review, integration project, and vendor relationship. Challengers, meanwhile, often win commoditized markets through sharper vertical positioning, faster onboarding, or markedly better customer support.

Ultimately, B2B buyers purchase reliable outcomes and low execution risk rather than software novelty. While product differentiation helps protect margins and fuel organic demand, strong go-to-market execution and a lower-friction buying experience regularly win deals without it.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
No, you can win without clear product differentiation, and B2B buyers often do. Gartner and CEB research (the basis for "The Challenger Customer") found that most B2B buyers see little meaningful difference between competing suppliers. Deals still get won, just on other grounds.

Those grounds include the buying experience itself: how well a vendor helps the buying group agree, reduces perceived risk, and makes the purchase easy to justify internally. Relationships and trust matter, as do existing footprint and integrations (the incumbent advantage), price and commercial terms, implementation and support quality, brand safety ("nobody got fired for buying IBM"), and simply being faster or more responsive in the sales cycle. Distribution and channel partnerships can beat a better product too.

Differentiation still matters a lot. It protects margins, makes demand generation and positioning easier, and wins against competitors who are otherwise equal. Without it you're usually competing on execution, price, or relationships, and those are harder to scale and easier to copy. So differentiation isn't strictly necessary to win individual deals, but it's very hard to build a durable, high-margin business without some differentiation somewhere: in the product, the go-to-market, or the customer experience.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
No, clear product differentiation is not always necessary to win B2B software deals. In mature or crowded categories, core functionality is often commoditized, so buyers frequently decide based on non-product factors rather than unique features. Companies routinely win with "good enough" products through superior distribution, stronger brand trust, existing vendor relationships, bundling, lower total cost of ownership, or a smoother buying and onboarding experience. Because enterprise buyers are risk-averse, familiarity, reliability, and responsive support often outweigh novel capabilities.

That said, winning without product differentiation shifts where you must excel and comes with trade-offs. Without a clear product edge, you typically have to compete harder on sales execution, marketing, pricing, or ecosystem leverage, which can compress margins and raise acquisition costs. Product differentiation becomes far more critical when you are a challenger without established distribution, creating a new category, or trying to command premium pricing. Ultimately, you can win without product differentiation, but you still need some clear commercial, operational, or relational advantage to give buyers a reason to choose you.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
You can win B2B software deals without clear product differentiation. If several products meet the buyer’s requirements, the decision may come down to price, an existing vendor relationship, a trusted referral, or which team can get them live by their deadline.

What matters is giving the buyer a reason to choose you. Two products can have nearly identical features, but one vendor might win by showing how it will handle a difficult migration and backing that up with a reference from a similar customer.

Product differentiation makes that reason easier to communicate and repeat across deals. Without it, you can still win, but your advantage may depend more on the circumstances of each deal.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
No. You can win a B2B software deal with a product that looks much like its competitors. Once several products meet the buyer’s requirements, the decision may turn on price, trust in the vendor, or how quickly the team can get started. A customer might buy another product from an existing vendor because the contract is already in place and a new supplier would take months to approve.

The distinction is between a unique product and a compelling reason to buy. Clear product differentiation helps when buyers care about the difference, but an easier or less risky purchase can be reason enough to win.
